overview: This Lagos record’s 1878 to 1914 window covers a port city already under British colonial rule, following annexation in 1861. It is not the founding date of Lagos or a period of independent kingship. Yoruba residents, Atlantic returnees, merchants, artisans and journalists helped shape the city as colonial government expanded around them.

periods.title: Within the Gold Coast administration
periods.summary: Lagos was administered with the Gold Coast until becoming a separate colony in 1886.

periods.title: A separate colonial administration
periods.summary: Lagos grew as a commercial and publishing centre. Residents debated how new services should be financed and who should benefit.

periods.title: Incorporation into larger Nigeria
periods.summary: Lagos was incorporated into Southern Nigeria in 1906. Northern and Southern Nigeria were joined in 1914.

items.text: Forest products replaced enslaved people as the leading exports, but slavery’s history remained visible in the population. Returnees and descendants of people taken across the Atlantic arrived from places including Brazil and Sierra Leone. Their skills, religious institutions and connections helped make Lagos a major commercial centre.

Older Yoruba houses commonly arranged rooms around a courtyard. The Afro-Brazilian sobrado offered another plan: several storeys, decorated stucco walls, elaborate windows and a central hallway linking rooms. Wealthy clients adopted this style, giving returning craftspeople a busy market for their building skills.

Andrew Thomas’s Ebun House, built around 1913, was so impressive that a nickname described people losing their caps while craning their necks to admire it. That joke comes from the historical account, not our imagination. The mansion made its owner’s success visible from the street.

The Shitta Bey Mosque opened in 1894. Its design adapted forms familiar from Brazilian churches for Muslim worship, and Catholic craftspeople helped construct it. Architecture records cooperation across religious lines as well as a prosperous Muslim community’s ambitions and connections.

sections.title: Learning about electricity, then arguing over the bill

items.text: Electricity entered Lagos classrooms before it entered ordinary street lamps. The CMS Grammar School taught scientific subjects, and an 1865 public lecture explained electricity and telegraphy with experiments. Learning about a new technology did not have to wait for a power station to arrive.

Residents wanted electric light but disputed a proposed house tax to finance it. African representatives, newspaper writers and protesters helped defeat that funding plan in 1895. Their objection was about who should pay; it was not simply rejection of the technology.

Electric street lights were operating by February 1898 after trial runs. African residents also obtained lighting in homes and religious buildings, although cost affected access. The system changed city evenings through both public lamps and private decisions about whether a household could afford a connection.

sections.title: Water for drinking, and waste to keep out

items.text: Nineteenth-century households relied on springs and wells, despite living beside a lagoon and the sea. Some wells were contaminated by sewage from nearby cesspools. Getting water was only half the problem; keeping human waste away from it mattered just as much.

In 1882, the colonial surgeon proposed covering wells, fitting pumps instead of lowering buckets on strings, and paving the ground around them. These were concrete ways to reduce contamination. Officials disputed the expense, so a sensible recommendation did not automatically become a working improvement.

Just after this map window, the Iju waterworks were formally commissioned on 1 July 1915. The scheme included public fountains and fire hydrants. A water network could supply a drink and help firefighters, but access expanded unevenly rather than reaching every resident at once.

sections.title: A city that read and wrote back

items.text: The Lagos Times of the early 1880s usually had four pages, about half occupied by advertisements and notices. Editorials, readers’ letters and local news filled the rest. Its pages mixed public arguments with the everyday business of selling things and announcing events.

“Iwe Irohin Eko” means “The Newspaper of Lagos.” Andrew Thomas began this Yoruba-English paper in 1888, charging twopence a copy. This Latin-script title follows the unaccented transcription in historian Nozomi Sawada’s study. It shows Yoruba readers demanding a place in the city’s print culture.

ending.text: The 1914 endpoint marks incorporation into the larger colonial state of Nigeria, not the disappearance of Lagos. Nigeria became independent in 1960. The city’s families, businesses, languages and institutions continued through those political changes, while its colonial history remained part of a much longer urban story.
